Area Forecast Discussion
National Weather Service Burlington VT
149 AM EST Fri Nov 13 2026

.WHAT HAS CHANGED...
As of 149 AM EST Friday...

No significant changes.

&&

.KEY MESSAGES...
As of 149 AM EST Friday...

1. Lingering snow ends early this morning. 

2. Widespread upslope snow showers Saturday, gradually tapering 
off Sunday. 

3. High confidence for dry weather and above normal 
temperatures next week.

&&

.DISCUSSION...
As of 149 AM EST Friday...

KEY MESSAGE 1: The center of the surface low has passed slightly to the 
east and backside cold air advection is causing the lingering rain 
to gradually change to snow. Snow levels have dropped to the valley 
floors in the Southern Champlain Valley and Marble Valley around and 
south of Rutland. However, snow levels are slightly higher east of 
the Greens as some of the surface cold air advection is being 
blocked, so they still range around 750 ft. So far, 1-3 inches looks 
to have fallen above 1500 ft in the southern Greens and the surfaces 
of the mountain passes have begun to become snow covered. Within the 
next couple hours, snow levels should reach the Connecticut River 
but the precipitation will end shortly after. Additional 
accumulations between 1-2 inches are possible around and above 1,000 
ft while mostly just a slushy coating is expected below. 
Precipitation will end by around 8 AM.

KEY MESSAGE 2: For the weekend, cyclonic northwest flow will prevail 
under an upper level low. However, for today, the region will be in 
an area of subsidence between shortwaves so it will be mostly dry, 
though a couple upslope flurries will be possible in the mountains. 
A potent embedded shortwave will pass south tomorrow and tomorrow 
night, bringing widespread showers. While they will be most 
concentrated in the typical northwest flow upslope areas, very 
marginal instability will develop in the lower 10,000 ft in the 
atmosphere due to cold air aloft and solar heating. This will cause 
the precipitation to trend more convective, especially Saturday 
afternoon. Therefore, snow showers will be able to survive crossing 
the terrain and should pass through the downslope areas like the 
Connecticut River Valley, though likely in a lighter form. While 
temperatures will rise above freezing below 2,000 ft, and likely 
reach 40 in the lowest points, temperatures will drop significantly 
in any of the showers. Therefore, even though consistent snow levels 
will likely only be down to around 1,000-1,500 ft, a period of 
graupel or even brief wet snow will be possible all the way down 
into the valleys. However, any continuous accumulations should 
generally be limited to above 2,000 ft. The showers will gradually 
become less and less widespread heading into Sunday, and they should 
be done by Sunday evening. Accumulations by the end should be in the 
1-4 inch range above 2,500 ft, with mostly brief coatings that melt 
below that. The lowest accumulating snow will fall Saturday night. 
Moisture off Lake Champlain will enhance the showers in the parts of 
the Champlain Valley and Greens, but the more convective nature may 
prevent the formation of distinct bands.

KEY MESSAGE 3: Deterministic and ensemble guidance are in strong 
agreement that an 2-3 standard deviation ridge of high pressure will 
be centered to the south and west of the North Country next week. 
Temperatures will start seasonably mild with highs in the 40s on 
Friday with temperatures warming a few degrees each day. Highs by 
Friday will warm into the mid 50s which will be 3-7 degrees above 
normal. Some of the deterministic guidance is trying to flatten the 
ridge on Friday with a strong shortwave but the likelihood of this 
scenario seems pretty low considering just how strong and amplified 
the upper level ridge is forecasted to be. Should the ridge break 
down, then it's possible we see some rain chances Friday into next 
weekend but again that's a very low confidence scenario as dry 
weather seems the most likely case at this time.

&&

.AVIATION /06Z FRIDAY THROUGH TUESDAY/...
Through 06Z Saturday...Conditions will steadily improve through the
morning as we see an area of low pressure move to the east.
Currently, we are seeing a mix of VFR at northern terminals and MVFR
at southern terminals. We are now getting into the tricky phase for
visibilities as temperatures begin to cool and allow for rain to
change over to snow. The idea is that MVFR conditions will be
possible south of KBTV through 14Z with an improvement to VFR
thereafter as precipitation taper off. However, there could be some
slightly heavier precipitation that could impact KRUT with brief IFR
visibilities due to falling snow. The remainder of the day will be
pretty quiet in terms of aviation with VFR conditions and light
northerly winds.

Outlook...

Saturday: Mainly MVFR, with local VFR possible. Chance SHRA,
Chance SHSN.
Saturday Night: Mainly MVFR, with local IFR possible. Chance
SHSN, Chance SHRA.
Sunday: Mainly MVFR, with areas VFR possible. Chance SHRA, Chance
SHSN.
Sunday Night: Mainly MVFR, with areas VFR possible. NO SIG WX.
Monday: Mainly VFR, with areas MVFR possible. NO SIG WX.
Monday Night: VFR. NO SIG WX.
Tuesday: VFR. NO SIG WX.

&&

.BTV WATCHES/WARNINGS/ADVISORIES...
VT...Winter Weather Advisory until 10 AM EST this morning for 
     VTZ018-019.
NY...Winter Weather Advisory until 10 AM EST this morning for 
     NYZ034.

&&

$$
